# Why 0-1 BFS exists

Section 19 used Dijkstra for nonnegative weighted shortest paths. If all edge
weights are only `0` or `1`, we can do better than a heap.

The idea:

```text
cost 0 edge: new state has the same distance, so process it very soon
cost 1 edge: new state is one layer later, so process it after current layer
```

A deque gives exactly these two choices:

```text
appendleft for cost 0
append for cost 1
```

# Recognition

Use 0-1 BFS when:

| Statement signal | Tool |
|---|---|
| every edge cost is 0 or 1 | 0-1 BFS |
| free moves plus paid moves | 0-1 BFS |
| minimize number of direction changes | 0-1 BFS |
| walking costs 0 and warping costs 1 | 0-1 BFS |

Do not use it when weights are arbitrary nonnegative numbers. Use Dijkstra.

# Deque primer

A deque supports both ends:

```python
from collections import deque
dq.appendleft(x)
dq.append(x)
x = dq.popleft()
```

C++:

```cpp
deque<int> dq;
dq.push_front(x);
dq.push_back(x);
x = dq.front();
dq.pop_front();
```

# 0-1 BFS template

```text
dist[start] = 0
deque = [start]

while deque not empty:
    u = pop front
    for edge u -> v with weight w in {0,1}:
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + w
            if w == 0:
                push v to front
            else:
                push v to back
```

This is Dijkstra specialized to two possible edge weights.

# The invariant

The deque is ordered by distance almost like a priority queue:

```text
states near the front have the smallest known distance
cost-0 relaxations stay at the front distance
cost-1 relaxations go to the next distance layer
```

So when a state is popped after its best distance has stabilized, all cheaper
ways to reach it have already had a chance to act.

# Worked example

Edges:

```text
1 -> 2 cost 1
1 -> 3 cost 0
3 -> 2 cost 0
2 -> 4 cost 1
3 -> 5 cost 1
5 -> 4 cost 0
```

From `1`:

```text
pop 1
  push 2 to back with dist 1
  push 3 to front with dist 0
pop 3
  improve 2 to dist 0, push front
  set 5 to dist 1, push back
pop 2
  set 4 to dist 1
```

The answer to `4` is `1`.

# Grid modeling

For Conveyor Grid:

```text
state = cell
edge = move to a neighboring cell
cost = 0 if movement follows cell arrow, else 1
```

For Warp Maze:

```text
walk to four-neighbor open cell: cost 0
warp within 5x5 square: cost 1
```

Both are standard 0-1 BFS once the states and edge costs are defined.

# Complexity

Every successful relaxation pushes a state into the deque. With adjacency
lists:

```text
Time:  O(V + E)
Memory: O(V + E)
```

For a grid with constant outgoing moves, this is linear in the number of cells.
For Warp Maze, each cell checks at most 4 walking moves and 25 warp moves, still
constant per cell.

# Common mistakes

```text
Using BFS and treating cost-0 and cost-1 edges equally.
Using Dijkstra correctly but more slowly when 0-1 BFS is intended.
Pushing cost-0 edges to the back.
Forgetting to relax a state if a better distance appears later.
Using 0-1 BFS on weights larger than 1.
```

# Local exercises

## A. Binary Weight Routes

Pure graph 0-1 BFS. Run once from the source and answer all queries.

## B. Conveyor Grid

Each cell's arrow creates one cost-0 outgoing direction and up to three cost-1
directions.

## C. Warp Maze

Walking is free, warping costs one. The result is the minimum number of warps.

# Submission checklist

```text
Are all edge weights exactly 0 or 1?
Did I use a deque?
Did I push 0-cost relaxations to the front?
Did I push 1-cost relaxations to the back?
For grids, did I check bounds and walls before relaxing?
```
# Exercises

Use A to recognize binary edge weights, B to encode direction as a state cost, and C to model warp moves explicitly. Test all-zero paths, all-one paths, and a case where FIFO BFS gives the wrong answer.
